candidates.title: Most Venture Capital Is Going To Companies That Are Founded Or Led By Billionaires
candidates.snippet: More than half of all seed- through growth-stage venture capital raised in the U.S. so far in 2026 went to seven companies founded or led by men who are already billionaires. Together, these companies raised more than $260 billion in equity funding in the first 10 months of the year.
candidates.text:

Most Venture Capital Is Going To Companies That Are Founded Or Led By Billionaires
Joanna Glasner
November 4, 2026
Joanna Glasner
jglasner
1
Shares
Email
Facebook
X
LinkedIn
The majority of U.S. venture capital nowadays goes to companies founded or led by men who are already billionaires.
This is not a difficult stat to unearth. So far this year, just seven companies raised more than half of all seed- through growth-stage investment. They’re mostly familiar names: OpenAI , Anthropic , xAI (now part of SpaceX ), Anduril Industries , Databricks , Prometheus and The Boring Co.
These companies raised more than $260 billion in equity funding in the first 10 months of the year. That’s just over 50% of the U.S. seed and venture investment over the same period, per Crunchbase data.
Founders and CEOs of these seven companies are also well-known — and exceptionally well-off to boot.
The world’s wealthiest men
Two founders are particularly famous. They are the world’s wealthiest men: Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos .
Musk founded xAI and The Boring Co., and also co-founded OpenAI, (though he has no known equity stake in the latter). And while outside investors funded these companies, Musk could have also afforded to do so himself.
Ditto for Bezos, who in 2025 launched the physical AI startup Prometheus, which raised $12 billion earlier this year. Bezos’ own net worth, meanwhile, is calculated at more than $350 billion.
AI’s leading names
The two highest valuation startups — OpenAI and the soon-to-be-public Anthropic — also have prominent billionaire founders and CEOs. However, they have mixed backstories to their wealth.
OpenAI co-founder and CEO Sam Altman primarily made his vast wealth through investments in Y Combinator startups, including Stripe and Reddit . Altman has said he does not have an equity stake in OpenAI beyond a sliver from an old YC round. Co-founder Greg Brockman , by contrast, has a larger stake in OpenAI that was reportedly valued around $30 billion earlier this year.
At Anthropic, meanwhile, all seven company co-founders have similar-sized equity stakes, and each is worth billions. This includes the AI giant’s most famous co-founder, CEO Dario Amodei .
Databricks, Anduril and others
Databricks and Anduril, meanwhile, both have founders serving as CEOs who have amassed billion-dollar-plus net worths during their tenures.
Databricks co-founder and CEO Ali Ghodsi has a reported $7.6 billion net worth , with the company he leads valued at around $190 billion following an August financing.
Anduril co-founder and CEO Brian Schimpf , meanwhile, has an estimated $1.5 billion net worth as a result of his stake in the $61 billion valuation defense industry disruptor. Co-founder Palmer Luckey , who sold his virtual reality startup Oculus to Meta for $2 billion in 2014 before starting Anduril, has an estimated $5.9 billion net worth.
Several other founders and CEOs of startups that raised some of this year’s largest rounds are billionaires too. This includes Wonder founder Marc Lore , Figure founder Brett Adcock , and Surge AI founder and CEO Edwin Chen , among others.
Billionaire categories
We can split the billionaires who founded this year’s most heavily funded startups into two broad subcategories. There are those who became billionaires through the startup that just raised capital. And there are those who were already billionaires through prior companies or investments.
Ghodsi, Amodei and Brockman fit in the first group. In the second group, of course, we can put Musk and Bezos, as well as Altman and Luckey, who became a 21-year-old billionaire following the Oculus sale.
Historically, neither billionaire type was a particularly common recipient of venture funding rounds. The term “unicorn” as a moniker for private companies valued at $1 billion or more only entered the lexicon in 2013, when this asset class became noticeably large. In prior decades, founders and CEOs mostly only hit billionaire status after their startups went public or sold in high-priced acquisitions.
Updating the venture archetype
But times change. And in tandem, our image of what a startup funding recipient looks like should evolve as well.
True, quite a bit of capital still flows to the stereotypical venture recipients: first-time founders or serial entrepreneurs whose prior companies didn’t make them fabulously wealthy. But a majority of venture funding now does not go to these classic startup types.
Instead, it goes to companies with valuations already high enough to warrant billionaire status for their stakeholders as well as ventures founded by men who are already billionaires.

candidates.title: Sector Snapshot: Construction Robotics Funding Soars To $1.6B, Tripling Previous Peak
candidates.snippet: Companies spanning construction and robotics have raised about $1.6 billion so far this year — more than 4x the $389 million recorded in all of 2025 — according to Crunchbase data. The surge was driven by three companies that raised the majority of the funding.

Construction companies are struggling to find enough workers. For startups, that means venture investors are pouring money into companies betting that robots can help close the gap.
Companies spanning construction and robotics have raised about $1.6 billion this year through Oct. 29 — more than 4x the $389 million recorded in all of 2025 — according to Crunchbase data. The surge was driven by three companies that raised the majority of the funding.
The broad trend: For contractors struggling to hire, the appeal of construction-oriented tech offerings is straightforward: They need to get work done and there aren’t enough skilled workers to do it. The AI-driven data center building boom is only adding to that competition for workers. Labor shortages remain the biggest cause of project delays, according to a recent survey by the Associated General Contractors of America and NCCER .
Some of the technology is already at work on job sites.
San Francisco-based Bedrock Robotics , this year’s largest funding recipient in the sector, said in August that excavators equipped with its autonomous systems were operating without human operators on commercial projects in Texas and Nevada.
The numbers: With roughly two months left in the year, funding has already surpassed the previous five years combined.
Companies spanning construction and robotics raised about $1.6 billion through Oct. 29, 3x the previous high of $506 million in 2021, according to our dataset that goes back to 2018. This year’s total is also more than 3x the 2021 high of $506 million.
So far, the funding surge reflects much bigger bets rather than more deals. The sector has recorded 30 rounds this year, compared with 28 in all of 2025. Bedrock alone accounts for $870 million across two deals — more than half of this year’s total. This underscores just how much a few large financings are impacting the recovery.
Austin-based Icon , which builds homes using 3D printing, also raised two rounds in 2026. It has raised nearly $800 million since its 2017 inception. A company spokesperson told Crunchbase News that the company has taken its technology from an experiment to “an in-the-field system that can build faster, with fewer people, less waste, greater design freedom and lower cost.”
To date, the company has built more than 270 homes and structures across five states and two countries. It says that it’s on pace to grow revenue by 4x this year.
“Early on, the question was whether a robotic construction system could build a good home,” the spokesperson wrote via email. “Today, the question is whether a company can deliver at volume, across geographies and project types, and improve its economics with each build. That’s only answerable with time in the field.”
Notable deals
Bedrock Robotics was the largest funding recipient in 2026, impressively raising $870 million across two rounds. The 2-year-old company, which converts existing heavy construction equipment into autonomous machines, announced a $600 million Series C in October led by CapitalG and Emergence Capital . That round, which valued Bedrock at $4.1 billion, followed a $270 million Series B in February led by CapitalG and Valor Atreides AI Fund .
Austin-based construction technology company Icon also raised two rounds, bringing its listed 2026 funding to $265 million. Its largest financing was a $200 million Series D in October led by Baillie Gifford and BlackRock , following a $65 million Series C in March.
Another $200 million round went to Gravis Robotics , based in Zurich, Switzerland, which develops technology to retrofit construction machinery for autonomous earthmoving and excavation. SoftBank led the company’s Series A in August, which valued the startup at $1 billion post-money.
Beyond those large financings, investors backed companies automating homebuilding and specific construction tasks.
Reframe Systems , based in Andover, Massachusetts, uses AI, robotics and automation to build homes. It raised $40 million in an August venture round led by Energy Impact Partners .
Amsterdam, Netherlands-based Monumental , developer of robots for on-site masonry and other building workflows, secured a $32 million Series B in July led by Khosla Ventures .
Meanwhile Las Vegas-based August Robotics raised a $30 million Series B in May led by Big Pi Ventures . Its autonomous systems serve construction, exhibitions, industrial fit-out and facility operations.
Belmont, California-based Gritt , which develops AI-powered robotic systems for infrastructure construction, followed with a $26 million Series A in July led by Obvious Ventures .
Sizable seed rounds also made the list.
London-based All3 , which uses AI and robotics to design, manufacture and assemble buildings, raised $25 million in April led by RTP Global . Origin , based in San Francisco, developing a general-purpose construction robot, secured $20 million in October, led by Accel and Zacua Ventures .
Exits
Acquisitions have dominated exit activity in construction robotics and related jobsite automation this year.
One of the largest disclosed deals was Carpinteria, California-based Procore ’s acquisition of DroneDeploy , a San Francisco-based platform that combines imagery from drones, ground robots and cameras to track construction progress and site conditions. Procore announced the approximately $845 million cash transaction in July and closed it in September.
Other buyers have focused on automating the work itself. In January, Oshkosh subsidiary JLG Industries acquired the core technology developed by Canvas , a San Francisco-based startup known for robotic drywall finishing.

Weekly Startup Funding Roundup: Fal Secures USD 1.3 Billion, Nooks Raises USD 500 Million
Fal raised USD 1.3 billion at a USD 16 billion valuation, while Nooks secured USD 500 million. Titan OS, Supa and Archera also closed rounds, showing strong investor focus on AI infrastructure, automation and cost optimization.
Written By:
Somatirtha
Reviewed By:
Manisha Sharma
Published on :
06 Nov 2026, 8:15 am
Updated on :
06 Nov 2026, 8:15 am
Copied
The global startup sector saw several significant deals this week, with AI, smart television technology, property management, and cloud cost optimization attracting investor interest.
AI inference startup Fal led the funding activity with a USD 1.3 billion Series F round, taking its valuation to USD 16 billion. Meanwhile, sales automation startup Nooks secured a USD 500 million financing commitment from General Catalyst.
Other notable deals included Titan OS raising USD 46 million, UK-based Supa securing USD 28 million, and cloud cost management company Archera attracting USD 15 million in Series C funding.
Fal Raises USD 1.3 Billion at USD 16 Billion Valuation
AI inference startup Fal raised USD 1.3 billion in its latest Series F funding round, doubling its valuation to USD 16 billion. Bessemer Venture Partners led the round, with participation from Nvidia, Sound Ventures and T. Rowe Price.
The company plans to use the capital to expand its AI inference infrastructure and meet growing demand for hosting video, image, and audio generation models. The investment also strengthens its ability to support open-source AI models as businesses increasingly rely on generative AI applications.
Nooks Secures USD 500 Million Funding Commitment
AI sales startup Nooks secured a USD 500 million financing commitment through General Catalyst's Customer Value Fund. The revenue-based financing facility will support sales and marketing expansion, business growth, and the development of new AI-powered products.
Its AI Revenue Agent Platform automates sales activities, covering processes from initial customer engagement to renewals.
Also Read: Weekly Startup Funding Roundup: Ramp Raises USD 1.85 B, Labelbox Secures Over USD 100M, Ultra Receives USD 62M
Titan OS Raises USD 46 Million
Smart TV operating system company Titan OS raised USD 46 million through an equity and debt financing round. Funds and accounts managed by BlackRock participated alongside existing investors Highland Europe and Mangrove Capital Partners.
The company will use the funding to enter new markets, establish partnerships, and improve AI-powered content discovery and advertising recommendations. It also plans to strengthen its operating system and monetization capabilities.
Supa Raises USD 28 Million in Seed Funding
UK-based property management startup Supa secured USD 28 million in seed funding through a combination of equity and debt. The round was co-led by 2150 and OpenOcean, with participation from KOMPAS VC, Actia Capital Partners and HEARTFELT. A major UK lender provided the debt facility.
Supa plans to expand its AI-powered residential property management platform, acquire local property management businesses, and automate administrative operations.
Archera Raises USD 15 Million in Series C
Cloud cost management startup Archera raised USD 15 million in a Series C round led by Pivot Investment Partners, with existing investor HighSage Ventures also participating.
The company will expand its Guaranteed Commitments offering and cloud cost management tools, including FinOps Agent and MCP. The funding will also support international expansion across North America, Europe, the Middle East, Japan and Latin America.
The week's funding activity highlights continued investor interest in AI infrastructure and automation, as well as technology platforms addressing operational costs and established industry challenges.

Laza Medical Raises Up To $160 Million In Series B Financing Led By GE HealthCare To Advance AI-Powered Cardiac Imaging
By Amit Chowdhry
Nov 5, 2026
Laza Medical Raises Up To $160 Million In Series B Financing Led By GE HealthCare To Advance AI-Powered Cardiac Imaging
Laza Medical, a medical technology company developing artificial intelligence-powered robotic imaging systems for cardiovascular procedures, has raised up to $160 million in structured Series B financing led by GE HealthCare. The round also included participation from returning investors Unorthodox Ventures, PA MedTech, and AMED.
The financing will support continued development of Laza Medical’s intelligent imaging technology, which is designed to improve procedural guidance, simplify cardiac interventions, and establish a foundation for future robotic-assisted cardiovascular procedures.
Laza Medical is a privately held portfolio company of Shifamed, a medical technology innovation platform founded by entrepreneur Amr Salahieh.
The company’s technology focuses on transforming the cardiac catheterization laboratory, commonly known as the cath lab, where physicians use imaging equipment to diagnose and treat cardiovascular conditions through minimally invasive procedures.
As cardiac interventions become more complex, physicians increasingly depend on advanced imaging techniques to understand anatomy, guide medical devices, and make treatment decisions.
However, the interpretation and coordination of multiple imaging systems can require specialized expertise, potentially increasing procedural complexity and placing additional demands on clinical teams.
Laza Medical is developing an intelligent imaging platform that combines AI and robotics to provide more consistent anatomical visualization and improve image guidance during cardiac procedures.
The system is intended to simplify workflows and reduce the variability associated with complex imaging processes.
By integrating imaging modalities and developing automated capabilities, the company aims to make advanced procedural imaging more accessible while supporting greater consistency in patient care.
The technology could also help extend specialized imaging expertise to a broader range of healthcare facilities as demand for cardiovascular procedures increases.
Laza previously completed first-in-human use of its real-time AI heart modeling software during a clinical study in 2025.
That milestone provided an opportunity to evaluate the technology’s potential to support ultrasound-guided cardiac interventions and improve clinicians’ understanding of anatomical structures during procedures.
The Series B investment also builds on Laza’s collaboration with GE HealthCare, which has experience developing medical imaging systems and technologies used across hospitals and clinical environments.
The companies share an interest in advancing imaging solutions that can integrate more seamlessly into cardiovascular procedures while supporting the longer-term development of robotic intervention systems.
Shifamed’s broader innovation strategy focuses on combining advances in medical imaging, artificial intelligence, and robotics to improve the efficiency and consistency of interventional care.
The Laza Medical System remains under development and is not currently approved for commercial sale in any geographic market.
With the new funding, Laza Medical intends to continue advancing its technology toward future clinical and commercial milestones while working to expand the capabilities of intelligent imaging in cardiovascular medicine.
KEY QUOTES:
“The future of cardiac intervention must be one where access, consistency, and quality of care are no longer barriers to better outcomes. Integrating imaging modalities so they work seamlessly together has the potential to redefine the cath lab, enabling more efficient workflows today and paving the way for smarter, robotic procedures tomorrow. We’re excited to expand our collaboration with Laza and work together toward this shared vision.”
Jyoti Gera, CEO Of Cardiovascular And Interventional Solutions, Advanced Imaging Solutions At GE HealthCare
“High-quality imaging is foundational to all successful cases. Consistent anatomic and spatial context simplifies procedures and helps clinicians navigate the anatomy with confidence and precision.”
Dr. Firas Zahr, Head Of Interventional Cardiology At Oregon Health Sciences University Hospital
“The cath lab is poised for a fundamental evolution, and intelligent imaging powered by AI will play a defining role in what comes next. As we reimagine the role of imaging in interventional care, we are grateful for the strong support from our investors, which validates our approach and reinforces our conviction that this solution will streamline processes, reduce variability, and ultimately improve the quality and reach of cardiac procedures.”
Amr Salahieh, Founder And Board Chairman Of Laza Medical

The funding will accelerate delivery of OcientAIQ Solutions for organizations running agentic AI analytics against dynamic, petabyte-scale data and critical-infrastructure workloads.
All existing investors participated, alongside several new investors. Returning backers included Greycroft, In-Q-Tel, Blue Bear Capital, Buoyant Ventures, PSP Growth, Pritzker Group Venture Capital and Eron Wolf. BOKA Capital is also joining Ocient’s board.
Ocient expects revenue to more than triple in 2026, citing demand from customers in industries that depend on continuously expanding, high-volume datasets. Earlier in 2026, the company formalized its India operations and Ocient National Security Solutions as dedicated subsidiaries.
CEO John Morris said the investment and investors’ expertise would help extend OcientAIQ to more customers as they scale their data and AI operations. He described the operational stakes: “Our customers operate at a scale where the speed, quality, and reliability of an answer can have significant consequences.”
Platform Architecture and Delivery
OcientAIQ Solutions are pre-built, industry-specific offerings delivered on the OcientAIQ Unified Data Platform. Each combines the platform with a Solution Pack containing curated agent skills, industry semantics and proven delivery patterns, framing outcomes in the terminology of the customer’s domain. Deployments are tailored to individual customer environments and provide components for agents and analysts to query and interpret data in real time.
The underlying platform unifies ingestion, governance, intelligence, business context and agent skills in one engine. Ocient says the design enforces access, policy and lineage controls over agent activity and runs analysis inside the engine rather than through a language model, making results reproducible and auditable while reducing data movement and token costs.
A dedicated OcientAIQ Solutions Delivery team designs, validates and deploys the offerings in customer environments. Its responsibilities extend from gathering requirements through production deployment and ongoing support. That team gives the funding a concrete implementation target: putting tailored systems into production and supporting them after deployment.

Ocient says its industry use cases analyze complete datasets without sampling. In cybersecurity, the software ingests network and security data as quickly as it is generated and makes it immediately queryable, helping teams detect emerging threats and trace where an indicator has appeared, and since when, across the full history.
The compliance offering is designed to help communications service providers meet regulatory obligations by retrieving every required record throughout mandated retention windows. Those records include call detail records and internet connection records, with lineage and traceability preserved across the retrieval process.
A third use case supports enterprises, service providers and government agencies building an AI-ready data engine that they own and operate in their own environment. The engine brings their largest datasets together so teams and AI agents can develop successive applications on the complete record rather than dividing the underlying information among separate systems.
The round ties Ocient’s growth plan to execution inside customer environments. Its approach pairs governed analysis of complete datasets with industry-specific packaging and hands-on deployment; the open question is how widely that delivery model can convert demand for high-volume analytics into production systems.

Mavria on November 9, 2026 unveiled its factory-built AI data-center business and disclosed $130 million raised to date across pre-seed and seed rounds. The total includes a new $100 million round led by Paradigm at a $1 billion valuation .
AMP PBC, Liquid 2, Critical Frontier and Dream Ventures also participated in the latest round. Mavria said it is already putting the capital to work securing critical supply chains, scaling manufacturing and expanding its team.
The announcement also introduces Terrain, the company’s first product. Chief executive Adam Blake said Mavria was formed to address a mismatch between the AI industry’s compute ambitions and the industrial capacity needed to build data centers and their supporting power infrastructure. The company’s response is to replace custom field construction with repeatable manufacturing, treating infrastructure as a product whose design and production can improve from one project to the next.
Terrain Integrates Power, Cooling and IT Systems
Mavria describes Terrain as a factory-built data-center platform for high-density AI compute, organized in standardized 5 MW blocks. Power, cooling, controls and IT pods are designed, integrated and tested as a standardized system before deployment.
That integration is central to Mavria’s commercial pitch. Instead of a customer sourcing separate modules and coordinating their assembly, Terrain is intended to provide an integrated, factory-tested product. Mavria says the approach is designed to bring compute online faster, with more predictable delivery and lower costs, although its initial product materials do not provide cost or schedule measurements.
The intended customers are frontier labs, neoclouds, developers and infrastructure owners. Their compute would run inside Terrain, while Mavria supplies the physical infrastructure needed to operate it. The company explicitly says it does not operate a cloud or sell compute, making its business distinct from providers that rent AI processing capacity.
Terrain 01 is being built in Houston as the first physical demonstration of the approach. Mavria describes it as in production, but full product details remain forthcoming. No separate commercial availability date was announced.
Manufacturing Capacity Is Central to the Model
Mavria’s operating model standardizes how infrastructure is developed, built and deployed through repeatable engineering, procurement and manufacturing. Development, procurement and manufacturing advance in parallel, while critical equipment, supply chains and production capacity are secured ahead of demand. The company says this is intended to reduce bottlenecks when projects are ready.
Writing after the announcement , co-founder Seth Cohen said Mavria was founded in June 2026 after the founders’ work inside government began in 2025. He set a target of deploying Terrain in weeks rather than months or years and linked faster deployment to less disruption for host communities. His longer-term ambition is for Mavria to manufacture products upstream from Terrain once it proves itself in data centers, extending the company beyond its first product.
The three founders, Blake, Nick Poradek and Cohen, previously worked together at the U.S. Department of Energy. Company biographies say Blake built more than 1,000 energy projects, sold a software business to Vista Equity Partners and advised the secretary of energy. Poradek sold a manufacturing company to Liberty Energy ( LBRT ) and then helped build Liberty’s manufacturing platform, while Cohen’s background spans nuclear policy, government and capital. The broader team brings experience in data-center engineering at NVIDIA and AWS, large-scale modular LNG manufacturing and infrastructure project finance.
For Mavria, the central question is execution: whether Terrain 01 can demonstrate that standardized, factory-tested data centers can be produced repeatedly and meet the company’s goals for deployment speed, delivery predictability and lower costs.

candidates.snippet: Robot-by-the-Hour Startup Tutor Intelligence Raises $75M Series B Wowtale
candidates.text:
AI has transformed the digital world, learning to converse and code from the internet’s vast record of text and images.
The physical world has no such record to train on. For robots to take over the lifting, moving and manipulation that keep factories and warehouses running, they need data from real work in real facilities.
Tutor Intelligence , a Watertown, Massachusetts robotics company that collects that data by putting robots to work, announced a $75 million Series B. The round brings its total capital raised to $117 million, following a $34 million Series A last December.
Tutor came out of MIT CSAIL and builds across the full stack: robots, foundation models and deployments. It places fleets of internet-connected robots in customer production sites, where remote operators the company calls “tutors” assist with tasks. Every completed task generates real-world experience data that trains Tutor’s own robot foundation model. Better models let the robots handle more work, which leads to more deployments. The company describes this as a network of intelligence in which each new deployment strengthens the entire fleet.
Its robots are called Sonny and Cassie. Tutor sells robot work the way businesses already buy labor: by the hour or by the pick. Customers make no upfront purchase and sign no long-term contract, and Tutor handles deployment, maintenance and regular software and model upgrades. The robots work in some of the largest U.S. manufacturing and logistics networks, handling goods such as breakfast cereals, snacks, candy, cosmetics, home goods and toys.
Josh Gruenstein is co-founder and CEO, alongside co-founder Alon Kosowsky-Sachs. Gruenstein says the models let robots do jobs they have never done before and make robots affordable on a new level, and that the company can hardly build robots fast enough to meet demand.
Andreessen Horowitz led the round. Union Square Ventures , which led the Series A, and Neo , which led the seed round, also participated. The company did not disclose its valuation or revenue.
The funds will support frontier robot foundation model training and the manufacturing and deployment of Sonny and Cassie. Tutor’s robots now work in almost four times as many facilities as a year ago, and the company is on track to have more than 1,000 robots under contract by the end of 2027, all built in and deployed from the United States. Nearly a third of organizations that received Tutor robots in the past 12 months were existing customers installing more of them.
Competitive landscape
Tutor competes with a growing field of physical AI companies. On the general-purpose robot model side, Physical Intelligence raised $600 million at a $5.6 billion valuation last November, Skild AI raised $1.4 billion in January, and Generalist AI raised a $400 million Series A at a $2 billion valuation in June, followed by another $200 million in August. These companies put the model itself at the center of their pitch.
Closer to logistics and manufacturing floors, Dexterity raised $95 million to develop physical AI, and Foundry Robotics raised a $100 million Series A last month for AI-run robotic assembly plants.
Tutor also trains its own foundation models, but treats them as one layer of a service. What sets it apart is the business model: supplying robot work by the hour or by the pick and feeding the resulting field data back into training.

Humble Robotics announced a $51 million Series A on November 5, 2026, led by Obvious Ventures to fund customer pilots, testing and validation, early manufacturing and a broader family of autonomous electric freight vehicles. Existing investors Eclipse, Energy Impact Partners and others joined the round.
Humble also distributed the announcement through Business Wire. The new round follows a $24 million seed round announced on April 21, 2026, when the company emerged from stealth with the Humble Hauler. Eclipse led the seed, with Energy Impact Partners and others participating.
Humble said at the time that it completed its first prototype in just under six months. Founder and CEO Eyal Cohen previously worked on autonomous driving, electric vehicles and logistics at Apple, Uber and Waabi. The founding team also included people from Tesla, Waymo and Cruise.
A Cabless Vehicle and Operating Service
Humble calls its approach unified autonomy: the vehicle, driverless intelligence and operations are designed together for dock-to-dock movements among ports, rail terminals, warehouses and distribution centers. The Hauler combines the functions of a tractor, trailer and driver. Its operating model includes full-service freight transport with 24/7 remote operational support and charging, and the vehicle is designed to unload directly at a dock.
Target applications include port drayage, full-trailer shuttles between factories and distribution centers, container moves inside rail yards and short legs between carrier terminals. Humble also plans to plug into existing charging infrastructure wherever possible.
The cabless Class 8 platform’s standard configuration moves 40-foot international and 53-foot US containers. A universal lock-and-twist interface is intended to support multiple vehicle configurations, and the platform uses an all-electric eAxle powertrain. Humble’s technical specifications list a 200-mile range and 55 mph speed.
L4-capable sensor pods combine automotive cameras, lidar and radar for 360-degree coverage. Redundant automotive-grade controls also form part of the vehicle’s safety architecture.
Vision-First AI for Regional Routes
Humble says its starting market, regional freight routes under 250 miles, accounts for 87% of US truck tonnage. The initial operating plan centers on short, repeatable dock-to-dock runs.
The company contrasts that choice with long-haul highway driving, which can require an 80,000-pound driverless vehicle to operate at 65 mph in rain, snow and fog, and describes retrofitted diesel trucks as risky and expensive for that task.
The Humble Driver uses a vision-first, end-to-end foundation model alongside safety constraints and rules based on customer sites. Its development combines photorealistic simulated scenarios with real-world safety testing. Humble says the system requires no mapping or predetermined route programming and that fine-tuning it for a specialized logistics environment takes no more than a few days.
Before making a move, the autonomy model produces a plain-language explanation of what it sees, what it is deciding and why. Humble says this reasoning directly shapes the vehicle’s action and makes each decision traceable and auditable.
Humble says removing the cab and using a 2,000-pound federal allowance for electric trucks create the potential for higher payloads without adding cost, while combining autonomy with electrification lowers per-mile costs.
The Hauler is intended to charge at a depot while it is loaded and run around the clock. Humble says hours-of-service rules cap a driven truck at 30% to 40% utilization.
The Series A moves Humble beyond its first prototype and into customer pilots, validation and early manufacturing. The central question is whether its integrated vehicle, AI and service model can deliver dependable dock-to-dock operations across the varied freight sites those plans are meant to serve.

Larridin has raised $30 million in Series A funding led by Pelion Ventures , bringing its total financing to $47 million. The company measures how AI spending translates into work across employees and software agents, targeting enterprises seeking clearer evidence of return on their AI investments.
Existing investors Andreessen Horowitz and Gradient Ventures participated alongside new investors GFT , W23 , Thayer , DG Daiwa Ventures , Alumni Ventures , and Cougar Capital .
In its November 2 announcement , Larridin said it has measured more than 2 billion AI sessions and tracked over 82,000 workflows. The funding will support product development and team expansion.
Connecting AI Bills to Business Output
The financial challenge goes beyond counting active users. An organization can pay for seats, consume model tokens, and run automated agents without knowing which activities improve its work. Measuring adoption shows whether tools are being used; measuring value requires connecting that usage to a useful result and the cost of producing it.
Larridin’s AI Impact product documentation describes combining invoiced licenses, token usage, and cloud-model costs with observed workflows and engineering-system data. It maps spend to departments and compares the work produced against that investment.
The methodology distinguishes AI-supported capacity from realized cash savings. Human-equivalent hours can estimate the work AI contributes, but their financial value depends on the baseline and how an organization uses that capacity. More available time does not automatically reduce a budget or staffing requirement.
That distinction is especially important when reading dashboard examples. Larridin explicitly labels its illustrative figures, including example ROI multiples and hours returned. Those demonstrations explain the calculation rather than establish a particular customer’s result.
How Workflow Intelligence Observes Work
The company’s Workflow Intelligence platform uses a browser extension and desktop agent to observe activity in applications selected by administrators. Larridin says it collects metadata such as active applications, their sequence, time spent in each step, and transitions between tools.
The product documentation says message bodies, document contents, screen recordings, and keystrokes are not collected. Views aggregate at team level by default, with individual views disabled unless enabled by administrators.
Those observations are grouped into workflows so teams can examine duration, repetition, friction, and where AI is involved. The platform ranks automation opportunities and tracks them through pilots and completed deployments against captured baselines.
Separating potential, modeled, and realized capacity matters here. A workflow identified as an automation candidate has not yet delivered the same benefit as one already running successfully in production.
Engineering Measurement Includes Quality and Review
Larridin’s Developer Intelligence offering connects engineering output with AI cost, delivery speed, and code quality. Its measures include output per $1,000 of AI spend, defect rates, and pull-request cycle time compared with a team’s own baseline.
The product also examines agent sessions and their captured steps, token usage, and estimated cost. A model-routing component lets organizations set cost and quality priorities for coding workflows and compare model choices.
That approach recognizes that generating more code is only one stage of delivery. Review capacity, verification, rework, and deployment can determine whether additional output becomes useful software.
The company’s AI Impact in Engineering Report for Q3 2026 illustrates the tension. Its analysis found the AI-assisted share of merged pull requests rose from 35% in April to 62% in September, and the funding announcement reports a 50% increase in median waits for an initial human code review. These findings describe Larridin’s measured cohort, rather than every engineering organization.
A Measurement Business Built Around AI Accountability
Larridin reports a 47% average increase in measurable team output and median first-year AI-spend optimization of $2.4 million across its customer base. These are company-reported results, separate from its illustrative product dashboards.
The leadership page identifies Russ Fradin as co-founder and CEO, Jim Larrison as co-founder and president, and Ameya Kanitkar as co-founder and CTO. Fradin and Larrison draw on earlier experience building digital measurement at Comscore. Their stated aim is to provide a comparable measurement layer for work performed with AI.
As Carta Chief Product Officer Vrushali Paunikar argues in a piece for Unite.AI on enterprise AI workflows beyond the connection layer , providing access to tools is only part of delivering reliable outcomes. Larridin’s focus is the evidence surrounding those outcomes: what the work cost, what changed, and where the next investment should go.

candidates.title: Yvonne Bajela is bringing $17M in fresh capital to Europe’s startup scene
candidates.snippet: Evertrue Capital announces $17M debut fund to back early-stage AI and fintech.
candidates.text:
Yvonne Bajela knew it was time to launch her own fund. She spent more than a decade as a VC, most recently at LocalGlobe and Impact X Capital Partners, where she made bets on now-unicorn companies like the fintech Wise, the insurance company Marshmallow, and robotaxi Mooves.
On Tuesday, she announced that her own fund, Evertrue Capital , officially closed an oversubscribed $17 million Fund I.
“After more than a decade backing founders who bet everything on their ideas, it felt like time to make a bet of my own,” she said. “I wanted the independence to act on those convictions and build something that reflected my own approach to investing.”
The firm, which has already backed seven companies, will focus on early-stage investing across the U.K. and Europe. The average check size will be around £350,000, she said, with plans to back at least 20 companies over the next three years.
Perhaps unsurprisingly, she said this AI boom helped her realize that this was the right time to launch her own fund. Not only has it changed the economics of launching a company, she said, but it has created new opportunities for early-stage investors like herself. “The ability to build has been democratized,” she said. “But the ability to build something enduring remains rare.”
As TechCrunch has previously reported, the U.K.’s startup scene is having a moment. King’s Cross, for example, is one of the world’s top AI hubs, while companies like Revolut, Synthesia, ElevenLabs, and the Bezos-backed CuspAI are redefining what it means to scale and attract success in the U.K. market. For someone like Bajela, this moment means there is an opportunity to snap up investments in the next generation of top British talent early. “I think more globally significant businesses will emerge from a wider range of starting points,” she said.
However, this is also a tough market for emerging fund managers. In the U.S., it has been described as a barbell market where capital is concentrated at the top and among firms led by those who already have solid track records. Things may be slightly rosier in the U.K., as PitchBook data through the end of September shows that emerging fund managers in this region raised $7.4 billion, already surpassing the $6.2 billion they raised in all of 2025.
Still, Bajela said fundraising was a grind. The hardest rejections weren’t necessarily the outright nos. “They were the ones that came after months of conversations and significant time invested, only for the answer to ultimately be no,” she said. “Time is one of the most valuable resources a founder has, and a prolonged process without clarity has a real cost.”
Still, she said the fund nabbed five institutional backers, including the British Business Bank and Basecamp, the fund-of-funds of the investment firm Phoenix Court, which is also home to LocalGlobe. Evertrue was part of the £400 million British Business Bank’s Investor Pathways capital initiative, which saw it distribute £90 million to 10 first-time fund managers. Bajela said Evertrue wanted to raise around $13 million but saw a lot of investor interest. She decided to turn down additional investors rather than expand the fund size.
“Fund size is a strategic decision, not a measure of success in itself,” she said. “I wanted enough capital to build meaningful positions in my highest-conviction investments without creating pressure to deploy capital simply because it was available.”
Around 80% of Evertrue’s LPs are U.K. based, with the rest scattered across Europe, Asia, and the U.S. She said her international LP base represents the relationships she’s built “over more than a decade investing across markets.” It also reflects the fund’s global ambition, she said, especially since so many British founders keep their eyes on a U.S. expansion; more than half her portfolio already operates in the U.S.
Evertrue will invest mainly across AI and fintech, she said, adding that she’s “particularly interested in people with a unique insight into a problem, an unusual ability to execute, and the ambition to build something much bigger than their initial product.”
“I also pay attention to the distance a founder has traveled, what they’ve overcome, and how that has shaped their perspective,” she continued.
She’s lived in Japan as a senior investment manager at Mitsui and started her career as an analyst at Goldman Sachs. Throughout her career, she said she’s seen how “widely distributed ambition and talent are.”
“I want Evertrue to be known for the quality of the founders I back and the businesses they go on to build.”

Brava Security Raises $15M Seed to Expand AI SecOps in North America
Published

By

Brava Security announced on November 4, 2026 that it was emerging from stealth with $15 million in seed funding led by F2 Venture Capital and Pitango, alongside a multi-agent platform designed to test whether security tools would actually detect an attack.
The round includes angel investors who are executives at Anthropic, Microsoft and Check Point . The capital is designated for Brava’s technology and growth across North America, including financial services, government and energy. Brava says it already works with Fortune 100 companies in retail, energy and hospitality.
The launch addresses a weakness in AI-driven security operations : an agent can make decisions about threats it recognizes while remaining unaware of attacks that its underlying defenses fail to detect. Brava identifies missing log collection, silently broken telemetry pipelines and flawed detection logic as potential causes.
Generating Evidence Without Running Attacks
Brava’s cooperating AI agents model attacker behavior and synthesize the telemetry an attack would produce across a customer’s environment without executing it. The process operates independently of existing detection rules and predefined tests, establishing what defenses should recognize before testing what they currently catch.
The platform works alongside the customer’s existing SIEM. Its detection-engineering function checks which attack steps current defenses recognize, identifies rules that stay silent, and writes missing detections in the SIEM’s own query language using only fields present in the generated evidence. It then replays that evidence to confirm that a real alert appears.
Scheduled game days repeat the validation after environmental changes. Evidence-backed maps show validated, partial, blind and missing-telemetry areas, while surfaced failures include broken detections, schema drift and dead log sources.
Aquarium, the investigation agent, accepts plain-English questions, plans and adjusts queries, and searches the SIEM, archived logs, EDR and cloud audit trails. Its reports link each finding to the underlying raw events.
The data-pipeline function sends events needed by detections to the SIEM and moves other data to searchable, low-cost storage rather than deleting it. Brava reports that this routing has cut SIEM costs by 65–85% across customers.
Reported Scale and Early Deployments
Brava says the platform supports more than 70 sources and destinations, including Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel, Google SecOps, CrowdStrike NG-SIEM , Elastic Security and IBM QRadar, with initial insights available 10–15 minutes after a SIEM is connected.
The company reports the following rounded daily measurements across customer environments: 2.4 trillion events read and fingerprinted, 1,100 attack techniques replayed, 3,800 detections retested and 140,000 fields mapped each day.
WELL Health CISO Iain Paterson said in a testimonial published by Brava that the platform helped his organization build and operationalize a new SIEM in weeks. “The continuous detection engineering makes sure that we never have dead rules and constantly have new detections being added,” he said.
Founders Behind the Platform
The founder biographies identify Idan Basre as co-founder and CEO in New York and Itay Gabbay as co-founder and CTO in Tel Aviv. Basre, a Talpiot alumnus, spent a decade researching attacker behavior in Unit 8200 before moving into product leadership at Microsoft Defender . Gabbay led joint US–Israeli DARPA AI research, developed autonomous AI systems and led enterprise AI security initiatives.
Brava’s expansion rests on a specific premise for AI-assisted security operations : automation depends on the quality of the telemetry and detection logic beneath it. The platform uses one evidence layer to validate defenses, support investigations and decide which data belongs in the SIEM. The open question is whether the reported detection and cost benefits can be sustained as customer environments change.

Venomics AI is harnessing India’s rich venom biodiversity and artificial intelligence to identify molecules with potential therapeutic applications.
Biotech startup Venomics AI has raised $2.7 million in a pre-seed round co-led by Speciale Invest and South Park Commons, with participation from Operators Studio, to advance its venom-based drug discovery platform.
The fresh capital will go towards expanding its Venom Atlas, a molecular dataset of animal venoms , strengthening its AI and laboratory screening capabilities, and hiring across biology, computational science and drug discovery.
Spun out of the Indian Institute of Science (IISC), the Bengaluru-based startup combines venom biology, AI and laboratory screening to identify molecules from animal venoms that could be developed into medicines.
“Animal venoms represent one of nature’s richest yet least explored sources of potential medicines, and at Venomics AI, we are combining cutting-edge experimental science with AI to unlock this extraordinary potential,” said Kartik Sunagar, founder and director of Venomics AI and professor at IISc.
The company, founded by Sunagar and Vinay Prabhu, combines Sunagar’s expertise in venom evolution and antivenom development with Prabhu’s background in machine learning and large-scale AI systems.
“Few people combine his deep understanding of these venoms with the access to study them. Vinay brings the AI depth to accelerate this bio-discovery,” said Arjun Rao, general partner at Speciale Invest.
The startup has established the initial architecture of its platform, joined the NVIDIA Inception programme , and been selected among the top five finalists for the 2026 Indo-Boston Biotech Bridge Award.
Prateek Mehta, general partner at South Park Commons, said, “Venom is one of nature's oldest targeting systems. It gave us Captopril and GLP-1s, and until now we've only been able to search one molecule at a time. AI changes that.”

A London-based startup building AI infrastructure for scientific drug discovery has received backing from the UK government’s Sovereign AI fund and Stripe CEO Patrick Collison.
Potential Sciences leverages AI, machine learning and quantum chemistry simulations to help researchers understand how molecules behave and interact.
It is pioneering a new approach, with an AI model focused on the fundamental laws of physics, rather than previous experimental data, the startup says.
It says this could make the AI calculations needed to design chemicals 100 times cheaper than at present.
The government’s Sovereign AI fund today confirmed it was backing Potential Sciences, as part of a raise in the tens of millions of dollars. The Sovereign AI fund is also committing compute capacity to Potential Sciences, which was founded in November last year.

The seed funding round also includes backing from Twin Path Ventures, Odyssey, Portfolio Ventures, Blue Wire Capital, rule30, Nauta Capital and Lightfield Equity, as well as angel investment from Collison and other angel investors.
Potential Sciences declined to disclose exactly how much was raised or its valuation.
Potential Sciences was founded by doctor Hatem Helal, a former Graphcore executive, the chip designed acquired by SoftBank, in 2025.
Sovereign AI Investment Partner Joséphine Kant said: "I first met Hatem in Cambridge, and he immediately struck me as a formidable founder.
